refuted.fact: FACT 35: SB 53 s22757.11(c) defines catastrophic risk as a risk that a frontier developer's development, storage, use or deployment of 'a foundation model' will materially contribute to >50 deaths / >$1bn property loss.
refuted.why: The statute says 'frontier model', not 'foundation model'. Verbatim from the cited leginfo page: 'a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people or more than one billion dollars ($1,000,000,000) in damage to, or loss of, property arising from a single incident'. 'Foundation model' and 'frontier model' are two separate defined terms in this same section (22757.11(f) vs (i)): a frontier model is a foundation model trained above 10^26 operations. Writing 'foundation model' widens the statutory trigger to every model and would put a wrong claim about who is covered into the article.

refuted.fact: FACT 11 tail: the '>50 fatalities' and '$1 billion' figures 'are the only two quantities in the whole document' (and the matching not_said line: 'Apart from 50 fatalities, $1 billion, six months, 12 months and 30 days, there are no numbers in it').
refuted.why: Refuted by the PDF I extracted myself. Other numbers in the FGF's 22 pages: the CBRN Tier 2 baseline 'relative to unlimited access to baseline of tools available in 2021' (p.10) — material, it is the benchmark year the whole CBRN Tier 2 test is measured against; 'we plan to release a more capable model in less than a month' (p.18); 'ISO 42001' (p.4); 'ISO 27001, 27017, 27018, and 27701' and 'SOC 2 Type II' (p.16); 'Regulation (EU) 2024/1689' (p.3); '27/7/365 incident response capabilities' (p.17); 'Appendix 2.2 of the Code of Practice' (p.18); 'Appendix B of the PF' (p.20). The quote of the definition itself is correct; only the blanket claim is false, and it is dangerous because the not_said version tells the writer the 2021 baseline does not exist.

unsupported.fact: FACT 50: 'Measure 7.6 requires signatories to provide the AI Office with an updated Model Report at least every six months', with verbatim_quote 'Signatories will provide the AI Office with an updated Model Report at least every six months.'
unsupported.why: The quote is a mid-sentence fragment that drops the condition governing it. Measure 7.6 actually reads: 'Further, if the model is amongst their respective most capable models available on the market, Signatories will provide the AI Office with an updated Model Report at least every six months.' As recorded it says every signatory model gets a six-monthly report; the Code says that only of a signatory's most capable models on the market. It also drops the three carve-outs that immediately follow. An article written from this fact would overstate an EU obligation.

unsupported.fact: FACT 26: OpenAI's model-report update cadence, presented as one rule ('We will in any event determine whether to update the Model Report for our most capable frontier models once every six months') plus three exceptions.
unsupported.why: The six-month sentence is quoted correctly, but the sentence that scopes the whole section is omitted. FGF p.18 opens: 'For models in scope of this Framework that are subject to the EU AI Act, if we have reasonable grounds to believe that the basis for considering the model's systemic risks acceptable has been materially undermined, we will update our Model Report as appropriate after completing a systemic risk assessment.' The update regime is written as an EU AI Act obligation, not a global OpenAI practice.

unsupported.fact: FACT 12: the FGF's risk assessment 'incorporates feedback from academic researchers, independent domain experts, industry bodies such as the Frontier Model Forum, and the U.S. government, the European Commission and other government agencies'.
unsupported.why: The quoted words are on p.5 but the qualifier is dropped. Full sentence: 'This process draws on our own internal research and signals, and, where appropriate, incorporates feedback from...'. 'Where appropriate' turns a commitment into a discretion, and the researcher's own FACT 27 rests on exactly that distinction ('We may solicit...').

unsupported.fact: FACT 17 framing: the cyber offense risk tiers are 'three tiers, described not numerically scored'.
unsupported.why: That gloss is the researcher's, not the document's, and the document says close to the opposite about itself: 'we have established a tier system that seeks to quantify model capabilities against cybersecurity threats and incorporates risk estimates and other suitable metrics. We use these measurable thresholds for decision-making' (p.9). The checkable statement is that the FGF publishes no numbers, scores or cut-offs for the tiers — not that it says the tiers are not quantified.

unsupported.fact: FACT 31: 'California SB 53 (Wiener) became Chapter 138 of the Statutes of 2025.'
unsupported.why: The cited leginfo bill-text page prints only 'CHAPTER 138'; 'of the Statutes of 2025' is not on it. The claim is true and I verified it on a different official leginfo page (codes_displayText for BPC Chapter 25.1 prints 'Chapter 25.1 added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 138, Sec. 2.'), but as recorded it is not traceable to the attached url.

unsupported.fact: FACT 37 tail: SB 53 s22757.12(b) 'is the statutory source of the 30-day changelog commitment in OpenAI's FGF'.
unsupported.why: Statutory text and the 30-day figure both confirmed, but the causal link is an inference. The FGF cites no section number and the statute never mentions OpenAI. It is also not a clean match: the statute requires publishing the modified framework plus a justification within 30 days of a material modification; the FGF promises 'changes and justifications for material updates documented in a changelog and published within 30 days of the update'. Write 'the same 30-day deadline appears in the statute', not a derivation.

unsupported.fact: FACT 52 tail: PF v2 'remains the version the FGF refers to as of 2026-09-16'.
unsupported.why: The FGF never names a version of the Preparedness Framework, never dates it and never links a PDF — only 'our existing Preparedness Framework (PF)' and 'Appendix B of the PF'. A blob last-modified header proves one file has not been rewritten in place; it cannot prove no v3 exists at another URL. Better support the researcher did not use: openai.com/news/rss.xml carries 'Our updated Preparedness Framework' at pubDate Tue, 15 Apr 2025 and no later Preparedness Framework item in 1,195 items.

unsupported.fact: FACT 7 framing: the FGF 'is designed to meet the baseline legal requirements of two regimes at once'.
unsupported.why: The document says 'Our FGF is designed to meet the baseline legal requirements of various frontier AI laws, including:' and then lists two. 'Including' is open-ended; the FGF does not say there are only two. The two bullet quotations themselves are verbatim correct.

additional_findings: MATERIAL AND MISSED — the TFAIA's effective date is verifiable first-party and is 1 January 2026. https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&division=8.&title=&part=&chapter=25.1.&article= (HTTP 200) shows 'CHAPTER 25.1. Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act [22757.10 - 22757.16]  ( Chapter 25.1 added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 138, Sec. 2. )' and prints '(Added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 138, Sec. 2.   (SB 53)   Effective January 1, 2026.)' under all seven sections. None is marked 'Amended by', so the chaptered text the researcher read is still the law in force on 2026-09-16 — itself worth recording, because a bill-text page is a snapshot of 2025-09-29 and does not prove current law. The date is central: OpenAI published the FGF on 2026-05-28, about five months after the statute took effect, and it is what the FGF's undefined phrase 'the Effective Dates of the TFAIA and the EU Code of Practice' points to on the California side. This page should replace or join the bill-text page in sources.

MATERIAL AND MISSED — the FGF's risk tier wording is largely lifted from the Preparedness Framework, which cuts against the researcher's framing that the two documents differ. Comparing the two PDFs I extracted: FGF CBRN Tier 2 ('The model can provide meaningful counterfactual assistance (relative to unlimited access to baseline of tools available in 2021) to novice actors (anyone with a basic relevant technical background) that enables them to create known biological or chemical threats') is word-for-word the PF's Biological and Chemical [High] threshold, differing only in the quotation marks around 'novice'. FGF CBRN Tier 3 is word-for-word the PF's Biological and Chemical [Critical] threshold. FGF Cyber Tier 3 is the PF's Cybersecurity [Critical] threshold verbatim but for 'OR the model can devise' vs 'OR model can devise' and 'high-level' vs 'high level'. FGF Cyber Tier 2 is the PF's Cybersecurity [High] threshold with 'provides substantial capability uplift to small organizations by' prepended. The FGF's CBRN prose about prioritising biological evaluations also tracks PF footnote 5 almost exactly. This is an observable textual fact from two first-party documents, not an inference about intent, and it does not conflict with the researcher's correct caution that neither document states a mapping. Editorially it matters: what is genuinely new in the FGF is Tier 1 (a band below the PF's High) and the legal framing, not the top two thresholds.

Missing qualifier that unbalances the article's central comparison. FACT 53 contrasts the PF's 'thousands of people or hundreds of billions of dollars' with the FGF's '50 fatalities / $1 billion'. The PF footnote does not stop there: 'By "severe harm" in this document, we mean the death or grave injury of thousands of people or hundreds of billions of dollars of economic damage. Our safety stack addresses a broad spectrum of risks, including many with harms below this severity. In choosing to set a high bar here, we aim to ensure that the most severe risks receive attention commensurate with their magnitude.' The researcher recorded the first and third sentences and dropped the second — the one that stops a reader concluding OpenAI ignores anything under thousands of deaths.

Missing: SB 53 s22757.11(c)(2) carves three things out of 'catastrophic risk' entirely — (A) information the model outputs that is 'otherwise publicly accessible in a substantially similar form from a source other than a foundation model', (B) 'Lawful activity of the federal government', (C) harm caused by a frontier model in combination with other software 'if the frontier model did not materially contribute to the harm'. As newsworthy as the 50/$1bn figure, and the article's second section is built on that definition.

Missing: SB 53 s22757.16 — 'The loss of value of equity does not count as damage to or loss of property for the purposes of this chapter.' This directly bounds the $1,000,000,000 figure the article will quote.

Missing: SB 53 s22757.13(h)-(j) is a federal-equivalence safe harbour. The Office of Emergency Services may by regulation designate federal laws, regulations or guidance whose incident-reporting standards are 'substantially equivalent to, or stricter than' the state rules; a developer that declares its intent to comply that way is 'deemed in compliance with this section', and failure to meet the designated federal standard 'shall constitute a violation of this chapter'. With s5(d) (act does not apply where it strictly conflicts with a federal-government contract) and s5(e) (nor where preempted by federal law), this materially limits the 'California law makes OpenAI's own words enforceable' framing in FACT 44.

Missing: s22757.14(d) — 'Beginning January 1, 2027, and annually thereafter, the Attorney General shall produce a report with anonymized and aggregated information about reports from covered employees'. FACT 42 records the parallel OES incident report and FACT 43 the Department of Technology review, but not this third annual report.

Missing: Measure 10.2 of the EU Safety and Security chapter has carve-outs the researcher did not record — 'For Frameworks, such publication is not necessary if all of the Signatory's models are similarly safe or safer models pursuant to Appendix 2.2. For Model Reports, such publication is not necessary if the model is a similarly safe or safer model pursuant to Appendix 2.2.' That is why the whole clause is conditional ('If and insofar as necessary'), and it explains why the FGF cross-refers to 'Appendix 2.2 of the Code of Practice' in its own six-month exception list.

Observation worth adding to not_said: Measure 1.1 of the EU chapter requires a Framework to contain, for each systemic risk with defined tiers, 'estimates of timelines when Signatories reasonably foresee that they will have a model that exceeds the highest systemic risk tier already reached by any of their existing models', supported by justifications, assumptions and uncertainties. OpenAI's published FGF contains no such timeline estimates and does not say which tier any model has reached. That is not evidence of non-adherence — Measure 10.2 asks only for a summarised version 'with removals' — but 'the public document does not tell you where OpenAI thinks its own models sit' is a checkable gap and a sharper version of the researcher's general not_said line.

Confirmed and worth keeping: the '27/7/365 incident response capabilities' string really is on page 17 of the FGF (I re-extracted it). The researcher's handling — record it in unverified_or_excluded, do not quote it, do not silently fix it to 24/7 — is the right call and should survive editing.

Verification I could add that the researcher could not: the EU document number 118119 was not guessed. Parsing the anchors on the GPAI policy page maps it exactly to the link text 'Safety and Security chapter (PDF)' (siblings: 118120 Transparency, 118115 Copyright, 118118 Model Documentation Form, 118312 Signatory Form, 124170 Vademecum). The leginfo bill_id 202520260SB53 resolves to precisely the claimed document and is corroborated by the codified chapter, so although it follows a constructible pattern I found no sign of fabrication. The cdn.openai.com PDF UUID cannot be pattern-guessed and returns the real 22-page document, so the 'found via search lead, fetched from the official CDN' route is acceptable under the BRIEF.

No disqualifying sourcing found.
